problem: Gaussian Splatting SLAM systems reconstruct geometry and appearance but carry no object-level semantics, and closed-set detectors (YOLO, Faster R-CNN) fail on unseen categories, so robots cannot be queried for arbitrary objects in unknown environments.
motivation: Robots in search and rescue, warehouses and similar settings need real-time reconstruction, object understanding and path planning to reach user-specified objects. Grounding DINO needs text prompts, which are unavailable in unknown scenes, and closed-set detectors misclassify or miss objects outside their training categories.
key_idea: Build a SplaTAM-style 3DGS SLAM map in which every Gaussian carries an object ID from GPT-4o-prompted Grounding DINO + SAM segmentation, then answer open-vocabulary queries by CLIP matching of the query to detected classes and localize the object with a 3D box, giving a goal for PRM path planning.
insight: An LLM/VLM (GPT-4o) can supply open-vocabulary labels to Grounding DINO, removing the need for predefined prompts. Qualitatively (Fig. 3), YOLO and Faster R-CNN miss guitar, backpack and computer and mislabel whiteboard as tv. Baseline 2, which matches query labels directly, is worse than the full CLIP matching plus keyframe pruning and re-segmentation (Precision 0.54 vs 0.61 in Office 2), so the matching step matters. The evaluation is small and self-defined, so the evidence is limited.
method: 3DGS SLAM backbone: SplaTAM-based RGB-D mapping with camera tracking by gradient descent on L1 color/depth losses, silhouette mask for densification, and per-pixel back-projection into Gaussians.
Open-vocabulary labeling: GPT-4o reads each image and outputs a list of object labels, which are passed to Grounding DINO for boxes and to SAM for masks.
Object ID embedding: pixels within each mask are back-projected and the corresponding Gaussians are tagged with a unique object ID.
Query matching: CLIP cosine similarity between the text query and the detected class names selects the best-matching class.

Search pruning: only keyframes containing the matched class are kept and grounded segmentation is rerun on them for fine-grained refinement; if the object is not found, the search expands to the remaining keyframes.
Localization: masked pixels are back-projected to a 3D bounding box, Gaussians inside it give a set of object IDs, and all Gaussians with those IDs form the object.
Path planning: PRM on a point cloud of Gaussian centers, with the object's box center as goal, run in Gazebo 11 / ROS2 with a drone.

numbers_note: Path-planning/navigation results are only shown qualitatively; no navigation success metrics are reported. The Replica object-query benchmark is the paper's own, not a standard one.
results: On three Replica scenes (10 queried objects each), Go-SLAM reaches Precision 0.60-0.62, Recall 0.70-0.73 and IoU 0.56-0.59. It beats Baseline 2 (no CLIP matching; Office 2: 0.54/0.58/0.44) and Baseline 1 (Faster R-CNN; 0.38/0.42/0.33). The abstract claims gains up to 17%, 27% and 35% in precision, recall and IoU.
limitations: Evaluation is small (three scenes, 10 objects each) with only ad-hoc baselines, no comparison to other semantic/language SLAM methods, and no quantitative navigation evaluation.
Depends on GPT-4o API calls and repeated Grounding DINO/SAM runs, so it is costly and its real-time claim is unsubstantiated; no real-robot experiments; dynamic scenes are claimed but not evaluated.
compares_to: Direct label matching without CLIP matching (Baseline 2)
